newsitem.title: HUNGARY: ALCOA PLANT IN HUNGARY FACES FIGHT ON DUTIES, FEES.
newsitem.headline: ALCOA PLANT IN HUNGARY FACES FIGHT ON DUTIES, FEES.

text.p: Officials of an Alcoa plant in Hungary that imports aluminium from Russia say an unexpected change in rules governing customs duties and fees from July 1 could cost the plant as much as $10 million a year.

The change could severely hurt the profit-making potential of the Alcoa-Kofem plant in Szekesfehervar, which has made losses all but one year since Alcoa bought a majority stake in 1993, plant officials said.
"Any changes in duties or anything that affects the cost of metal purchases...have a very serious effect on our business," Alcoa-Kofem general manager Ralph Matera told Reuters.

Matera said Alcoa-Kofem now pays duties and fees of roughly nine percent on the 100,000 tonnes of aluminium it imports every year, but is able to draw back most of that because the bulk of the aluminium is re-exported to Western Europe, primarily Germany.
Under a change to bring Hungarian regulations in line with EU practices, the government plans to end the draw back provision as of July 1, plant officials and diplomats said.
Matera said fees and duties could add up to $10 million a year for Alcoa-Kofem at current aluminium prices of about $1,650 per tonne.
"When Alcoa came here we didn't ask for any duty benefit, we never asked for anything," Matera said.
"But now we're in a situation where they're going to take $10 million out of our pockets and we're saying that's a little too steep. We can't deal with that, you've got to help us."
Alcoa-Kofem has contacted the finance minister and the minister of trade and industry concerning the matter.
U.S. Ambassador Donald Blinken also has written a letter to Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy requesting that the Hungarian government review the matter, an embassy official said.
"The ambassador sent a letter in support of Alcoa's appeal for a review for an exemption," John Fogarasi, the embassy's senior commercial officer, said.
"In other words, he has asked consideration be given to Alcoa's request."
Adam Peto, assistant to finance ministry state secretary Tibor Draskovics, said the ministry was aware of Alcoa-Kofem's concern about the change in regulations.
"We are aware of this issue and we are looking into the problem," he said. "We are thinking about a solution."
